JEE prep amplified my depression 10-fold (which I developed during lockdown), as well as causing paranoia due to burnout.

I enjoyed the preparation. I enjoyed learning and competitive nature of the preparation. I enjoyed studying. My family was really chill no pressure at all. But I wasn't sure of engineering. I did clear JEE mains but I didn't wanted to be an engineer so I dropped it and pursued CA. I won't change anything. It gave me critical thinking. I like where I am today. I still love physics and chemistry but only upto what's taught till 12th.

So basically, I didn't get my dream college cuz of some stupid eligibility criteria I couldn't meet because of my location.
The main reason I even wanted to do JEE was dead simple — I just wanted to earn good money and buy all the shit I wanted. At the end of the day, it was all about money, and back in 2022, JEE felt like the only fucking path to actually make that happen.
But looking back, the JEE prep did teach me a lot — discipline, hard work, motivation, time management, all that self-hate and self-love bullshit, understanding my weaknesses and strengths. That mental toughness and the physical stamina I built during those crazy years is actually helping me right now in my job as an AI automation specialist at a US-based digital marketing company.
I don't use integration formulas or Newton's laws or any of that shit in my daily work, but the focus, problem-solving mindset, and resilience I gained is helping me learn fast and do decent in this fast-changing field.
Honestly though, in today's super fast AI world, I wouldn't recommend doing full JEE prep to most people in this generation. (Before 2022, I probably would've said yeah go for it.)
If your only goal is to make money and that's it, then this is what I'd do instead: Don't waste 2-3 years grinding on stuff you'll probably never use again. Just start learning practical skills that actually pay right now — like video editing (especially with AI tools), social media management, digital marketing, content creation, prompt engineering, basic SEO, sales, 3D modelling, or even doing freelance virtual assistance stuff. New tools and opportunities keep popping up every couple of weeks in this space.
If you have literally zero choice or your parents won't allow anything else, then okay, JEE is still a solid disciplined path. But otherwise, in this AI world, you don't have time to spend years building mental strength on topics you'll never apply later. Better to put that same hard work into skills you'll actually use every single day in your career.
